item.title: Chaotic-Periodic Alternation in a Financial System with Double Delays
item.description: arXiv:2611.14702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we present the chaotic-periodic alternation phenomenon within a three-dimensional nonlinear financial system subjected to Pyragas-type time-delayed feedback, as well as the lag effect of the interest rate in the price index dynamics. Through numerical analysis, transitions to chaos, including period-doubling cascades, period-halving routes, and incommensurable-period dynamics are characterized. The emergence of chaotic-periodic alternation are found and described. Results suggest that minor timing misalignments in the inner dynamics of a financial system, as well as those considered in the feedback loop can induce systemic volatility.
item.dc:creator: Jes\'us Salinas-Gutierrez, V\'ictor F. Bre\~na-Medina, Marcos \'Angel Gonz\'alez-Olvera, Anah\'i Flores-P\'erez

item.title: Chaos without Local Spectral Instability in a Kicked Oscillator
item.description: arXiv:2611.15525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A damped harmonic oscillator kicked by a pulsed periodic potential can be chaotic although every local Jacobian has eigenvalues inside the unit circle. Damped rotation between kicks lets non-normal shears of opposite curvature compound, so ordered products of contracting Jacobians amplify perturbations. We derive the exact joint spectral radius of the Jacobian family and an exact Lyapunov-exponent decomposition showing how this geometric pumping overcomes dissipation. The proposed mechanism can be realized with laser-cooled trapped ions in a pulsed optical lattice.
item.dc:creator: Vincenzo Citro, Giuseppe Petrillo, Didier Sornette

item.title: Basin Adjacency Graphs: A New Approach to Characterizing Basins of Attraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.15626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fractal basins of attraction are commonly characterized through resolution-dependent measurements, such as box-counting methods, uncertainty exponents, and basin entropy. Here we introduce a different approach based on the adjacency relations between connected components of the basins, without retaining their detailed spatial geometry. A finite-resolution basin diagram is represented by a graph with one vertex per connected component and edges linking adjacent components belonging to different basins. We investigate how the number of vertices scales with the spatial resolution $N$, following a power law $N^\alpha$ in the systems considered. Under suitable assumptions, the exponent $\alpha$ is related to the Kor\v{c}\'ak exponent of the component-size distribution and can coincide with the box-counting dimension of the basin boundary when its fractal structure arises from the proliferation of components. The graph also provides adjacency-based diagnostics that may help characterize basin configurations exhibiting the Wada property. We illustrate the approach using idealized Sierpi\'nski constructions, the Newton and relaxed Newton families, and three dynamical systems with previously established Wada basins.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre Wagemakers, Aryan Srivastava, Miguel A. F. Sanju\'an

item.title: Directed Wada cascade in systems with discrete scale invariance
item.description: arXiv:2611.15848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dissipative systems whose equations are unchanged by a dilation can host an infinite ladder of attractors, each shell an exact magnified copy of the one before. Since such dynamics cannot tell a magnification from its inverse, the natural expectation is that these basins are maximally entangled, with every boundary point lying on the boundary of all of them, following the Wada property. We find that this expectation fails, and fails in a precise way. Dilation covariance and a single trapping region together bound which basin boundaries a point can lie on, and the bound depends only on its distance to the origin. No point lies on the boundary of all of them. The basins on whose boundary a point does lie are the deeper ones, as we prove for the stable manifolds of the boundary saddles and support numerically for the rest of the boundary, so the boundaries nest in one direction only. We call this structure a directed Wada cascade, and the standard Wada tests, as usually applied, do not detect it. It arises in maps whose nonlinearity is a log-periodic modulation of a homogeneous function, because the same periodicity builds the ladder through mode locking and confines the orbits. We show the cascade in maps that differ in invertibility, nonlinearity, scaling exponent and dimension, and in a flow.
item.dc:creator: P. Haerter, R. L. Viana, M. A. F. Sanju\'an, I. L. Caldas

item.title: Tendex Lines and Short-Time Deformation: The Geometry of Lunar Tides
item.description: arXiv:2611.16083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tendex lines and the stretchlines and squeezelines of Lagrangian coherent structure theory share a geometric construction: they integrate eigenvector fields of symmetric tensors. We connect their dynamical interpretations through the short-time deformation of particles released with zero initial velocity relative to a freely falling reference in an autonomous gravitational field. The leading departure of the Cauchy--Green tensor from the identity is quadratic in time and equals the tidal tensor multiplied by the squared observation time. The tidal tensorlines therefore give the limiting principal stretching and squeezing directions. For the planar lunar field, these tensorlines are radial lines and concentric circles centered on the Moon. The same tidal tensor defines a Lorentzian metric whose null directions have no quadratic change in line-element length. Its null geodesics are logarithmic spirals, describing the short-time limit of finite-time unit-stretch geometry. Near Earth, the principal tensorlines clarify the two outward tidal tendencies, while the null directions distinguish vanishing leading extension from vanishing relative acceleration.
item.dc:creator: F. J. Beron-Vera

item.title: Stochastic-layer width as an order parameter for the integrability-to-chaos transition in the bouncer model
item.description: arXiv:2611.16804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The transition from integrable to chaotic dynamics in the conservative bouncer model is investigated within the phenomenological framework of continuous phase transitions. In the integrable limit, $\epsilon = 0$, the action variable is conserved and the phase space is completely foliated by horizontal invariant curves. Introducing a weak periodic perturbation, $\epsilon > 0$, destroys resonant tori and generates localized stochastic layers around the fixed points of the mapping, even at parameter values where global phase-space portraits appear predominantly regular. By dividing the angular domain into discrete bins and extracting the extreme action values visited by a single chaotic trajectory, the upper and lower boundary curves of the stochastic layers surrounding the period-one fixed points $(\pi, 0)$ and $(\pi, \pi)$ are reconstructed numerically. For the fixed point $(\pi, 0)$, the stochastic layer develops in the region $V \geq 0$ and is bounded by two curves, whereas around $(\pi, \pi)$ the layer extends across both sides of the line $V = \pi$ and requires a four-boundary characterization. In both cases, the mean width of the stochastic layer acts as a geometrical order parameter that vanishes continuously as $\epsilon \to 0$ and obeys a power-law scaling proportional to $\epsilon^{\alpha}$, with exponents $\alpha = 0.496 \pm 0.001$ around $(\pi, 0)$ and $\alpha = 0.496 \pm 0.006$ around $(\pi, \pi)$. The associated response function diverges in the integrable limit, providing clear numerical evidence of critical behavior belonging to the $\alpha \simeq 1/2$ universality class of weakly perturbed Hamiltonian systems.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Borin, Arturo C. Marti, Edson D. Leonel

item.title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
item.description: arXiv:2611.15344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Ross Ah-Weng, Peter V. Coveney

item.title: Antiperiodicity in the Duffing--Holmes oscillator: symmetry origin, parity selection, and transitions
item.description: arXiv:2607.05604v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the origin and distribution of antiperiodicity --- oscillations satisfying $x(t+T)=-x(t)$ --- in the periodically driven Duffing--Holmes oscillator, combining analytical arguments with extensive numerical exploration. Antiperiodic orbits are precisely the periodic orbits invariant under the half-period shift symmetry $S:(x,\dot{x},t)\mapsto(-x,-\dot{x},\,t+T_d/2)$ of the equations of motion, with $T_d$ the driving period. We map the antiperiodic regions across the plane spanned by the amplitude and the frequency of the forcing, together with the periodic and chaotic domains and the potential wells visited by each orbit. The invariance under $S$ imposes a parity selection rule, verified without exception across our parameter sweeps: antiperiodic orbits lock to the drive only at odd multiples of the forcing period. Periodic orbits that lack the antisymmetry occur instead as conjugate pairs related by $S$, each orbit being the point reflection of its twin. Following the approach of Swift and Wiesenfeld, who established that in this class of systems a symmetric orbit cannot undergo a direct period doubling, we quantitatively analyze the exit from the antiperiodic regime and explicitly identify the two codimension-one bifurcations through which it takes place: a supercritical pitchfork, in which the antiperiodic orbit splits into two conjugate, symmetry-broken orbits, and a saddle-node bifurcation with an antiperiodic saddle, in which the antiperiodic orbit disappears with its symmetry intact. Antiperiodicity thus emerges as the orbit-level manifestation of a discrete symmetry of the driven system.
item.dc:creator: Arturo C. Marti, Edson D. Leonel

item.title: Globalizing the Carleman linear embedding method for nonlinear dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2510.15715v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Carleman embedding method is a well-known technique for linearizing a system of nonlinear differential equations, but fails to converge in regions where there are multiple fixed points. We prove that the need for the solution to be expressible as a convergent Taylor series of the initial conditions leads to restrictions on the stability and convergence of the Carleman algorithm. Inspired by this realization, we propose and test three different versions of a global piecewise Carleman embedding technique, based on partitioning space into multiple regions where the center and size of the embedding region are chosen to control convergence. The first method switches between local linearization regions of fixed size once the trajectory reaches the boundary of the current linearization chart. During the transition, the embedding is reconstructed within the newly created chart, centered at the transition point. The second method also adapts the chart size dynamically, enhancing accuracy in regions where multiple fixed points are located. The third method partitions the state space using a static grid with precomputed linearization charts of fixed size, making it more suitable for applications that require high speed. All techniques are numerically tested on multiple integrable and chaotic nonlinear dynamical systems demonstrating their applicability for problems that are completely intractable for the standard Carleman embedding method. Simulations of chaotic dynamical systems such as various types of strange attractors demonstrate the power of the adaptive methods. However, global Carleman methods face fundamental limitations when simulating chaotic nonlinear systems on quantum computers due to overhead during nonlinear remapping.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Novikau, Ilon Joseph

item.title: Ulam Approximation for Nonautonomous Systems: Equivariant Measures and Linear Response
item.description: arXiv:2606.02889v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Despite the prevalence of nonautonomous systems in applications, their statistical properties are much less understood than in the autonomous setting. Building on recent results on response theory for nonautonomous systems, we study the approximation of equivariant families and of their linear response by Ulam-type finite-dimensional reductions. First, we show that coarse-graining procedures associated with the classical Ulam method, and more generally with suitable finite-element projections, such as those often associated with the Koopman/Kolmogorov operator-informed analysis of dynamical systems, provide rigorous approximation of equivariant families for sequential systems with memory loss. Second, for systems whose transfer operators are regularising, we prove that the linear response of the reduced finite-state Markov model converges to the projected linear response of the original system. We illustrate the results with numerical experiments on simple but representative time-dependent diffusive models. These results provide a rigorous foundation for the use of Markov approximations in the study of statistical properties of nonautonomous complex systems which almost invariably relies on finite-scale and finite-precision descriptions of their states and dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Galatolo, Valerio Lucarini, Isaia Nisoli

item.title: Coupled multiscale paleoclimate reconstruction with four-dimensional variational data assimilation
item.description: arXiv:2608.19469v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Paleoclimate archives extend climate knowledge beyond the instrumental era, registering different seasons, variables, time averages, and memory lengths. A longstanding problem is to integrate these heterogeneous sources of information within a unified methodology. Here we present a new data-assimilation framework, Last Millennium Reanalysis 4D-Var (LMR4D-Var), which reconstructs climate trajectories from these heterogeneous datasets while balancing errors in the model, observations, and initial conditions. We compare results using LMR4D-Var to assimilate proxies from PAGES2k, Temp12k, and borehole temperature profiles without treating them as instantaneous equivalents. Instrumental validation demonstrates that LMR4D-Var achieves the highest skill in reconstructing global mean temperature among existing reconstructions. Borehole assimilation preserves skill against withheld annually resolved records, increases agreement between reconstructed 300--2000-m ocean heat content (OHC) and independent estimates, and yields a cooler reconstructed Little Ice Age ocean. Modern 130-year OHC trends in the 0--300-m and 300--2000-m layers exceed their respective reconstructed pre-1870 Common Era trend distributions. Results for Temp12k demonstrate assimilation of decadal-to-millennial records and the potential for Holocene and deeper-time applications with suitable emulators.
item.dc:creator: Zilu Meng, Gregory J. Hakim, Julien Emile-Geay, Tanaya Gondhalekar, Eric J. Steig

item.title: Predicting tipping points: The many shades of non-equilibrium and catch-22s of early-warning
item.description: arXiv:2609.10378v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The potential of crossing climate tipping points has reached the attention of many researchers and the general public. On the one hand, the basis for this concern is strengthening, with simulations showing abrupt transitions that may occur even for moderate greenhouse gas emission scenarios. On the other hand, our understanding of what constitutes such transitions mathematically is becoming more nuanced. This leads to challenges for the fidelity of early-warning signals (EWS), which accompany bifurcations in systems that closely track a slowly changing steady state. Different kinds of out-of-equilibrium dynamics in a rapidly changing climate, as well as chaos, blur the notion of a critical tipping threshold and imply limits in predictability. Using EWS to detect loss of local stability from data requires careful evaluation in the high-dimensional system, and may have limited predictive power in a highly multistable climate, where there is more than a single, well-known alternative state. This calls for new methods using non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and dynamical systems to efficiently probe the global stability properties of climate models and observations.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Lohmann

item.title: Round-Based Contagion Generates Chaos from Oscillatory Dynamics: A Two-Stage Contagion Map
item.description: arXiv:2611.08353v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many social processes unfold in rounds, such as elections, meetings or turns of a game, in which individuals update synchronously. We show that this round structure can turn a regular oscillation into chaos. In Katriel's differential equations, two-stage contagion (adoption after two contacts with adopters) combined with population turnover produces bistability and relaxation oscillations, but no chaos. From the elementary reactions we derive a deterministic map $F_\tau$ for a large population updated in rounds of length $\tau$: each individual makes at most one transition per round, events compete as exponential risks, and adoptions take effect from the next round. Katriel's equations are recovered as $\tau\to0$. For short rounds the map follows the relaxation cycle, and the phase of successive outbreaks obeys a circle homeomorphism, which excludes chaos. As the rounds lengthen, this circle map loses invertibility and the invariant curve breaks down; once a round lasts about two mean adoption times, comparable to the duration of an outbreak, the attractor is chaotic, while Katriel's equations remain on a periodic relaxation cycle. With the probability $p$ of adoption after a single contact as bifurcation parameter, the map goes from extinction through a window of chaos to a stable equilibrium; for $\beta/\gamma=46$, $\mu/\gamma=0.002$, $\gamma\tau=5.5$ the window is $0.023\le p\le0.056$, bounded by the invasion threshold and by a boundary crisis, whereas Katriel's equations oscillate for $0.022<p<0.41$. Chaos is supported by the Lyapunov spectrum (Kaplan--Yorke dimension $1.81$), the correlation dimension, the 0-1 test, ordinal-pattern complexity, saddle periodic orbits and a horseshoe of the phase map. One-stage contagion, $p=0$ and permanent adoption showed no chaos.
item.dc:creator: Francisco J. Mu\~noz, Juan Carlos Nu\~no, Luca Meacci
